newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu's call for truce rejected by rebels.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu's call for truce rejected by rebels.

text.p: Zaire rebels rejected on Friday ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's call for a truce, saying he was only trying to buy time and his return home made no difference.
Asked about Mobutu's ceasefire call and return to Kinshasa from France, rebel political commissioner Deo Bugera said: "We do not receive Mobutu's orders. If Mobutu comes back it makes no difference.
"We are going to liberate our people. He always wants to buy time. But we will not play his game."

Bugera was speaking in the northeastern Zairean capital of Kisangani, captured by the rebels last weekend. Rebel leader Laurent Kabila was flying on Friday from rebel headquarters in Goma to Kisangani for his first visit since its fall.
Diplomats said United Nations special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was expected to arrive in Kisangani later on Friday after talks with Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni to press Kabila for a truce.
The rebel leader says he wants negotiations with Mobutu, or his representative, before any ceasefire and he will only talk about how the 66-year-old ruler plans to step down from power.
Mobutu left France on Friday to return to Kinshasa.

The rebels have seized more than a fifth of Zaire since launching their revolt in the east and Kabila says his forces will press on to the diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi and Zaire's second city Lubumbashi.
Mobutu, who is suffering from cancer, issued an appeal late on Thursday in a statement from his villa on the French Riviera, calling for a ceasefire and urging the Zairean people "to rise together".
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga, has said his father did not rule out talks with the rebels led by Laurent Kabila but this had to be in agreement with the government and parliament.

Mobutu said he welcomed all regional and international efforts to bring peace, adding: "There must be a ceasefire to put an end to the sufferings which our people are enduring and to allow humanitarian aid to be sent in safe conditions to those who need it."

Mobutu's statement was hand-written, apparently in reaction to a U.S. official who said in Washington this week that from reports he received the president "can barely write his name, so the guy clearly isn't going to be around that much longer."
